Distribution Transformer & Power Quality Monitoring

A compact sensor for transformer oil, and a Class A analyser for the quality of supply.

Distribution networks hold thousands of transformers, each too small to justify a full monitoring system, and they deliver the voltage that customers actually receive. Two measurements cover this level.

Plan a technical meeting Product datasheets

01Two measurements

One looks into the transformer. One looks at the network.

A

A · Distribution transformer

Oil condition, one unit at a time.

The oil in a transformer insulates and cools. Over years it ages and takes up moisture, and both lower its ability to withstand voltage. In a large power transformer this is followed with laboratory samples and dedicated monitors. A distribution network has too many units for that.

The practical answer is one compact sensor per unit, sitting in the oil and reporting its condition continuously. It does not give the depth of a laboratory analysis. It gives a continuous indication for assets that otherwise have none.

B

B · Supply point / busbar

Quality of supply, at a connection point.

Power quality is not the condition of one asset. It is a property of the network, measured at a connection point: how close the delivered voltage is to a steady sine wave of the right magnitude and frequency.

Disturbances come from both directions. Faults and switching elsewhere on the network cause dips. Non-linear loads such as converters, drives and power supplies draw distorted current and cause harmonics. A fixed analyser at the connection point records what happened, when, and for how long.

Power quality is a network property measured at a connection point, not a condition of one asset.

02What it detects

Three signs in the oil. Seven events on the voltage.

AIn the transformer

  1. 01Falling dielectric strength of the oil
  2. 02Rising moisture
  3. 03Hydrogen as a sign of a developing fault

The method in general: online oil-condition sensing. What a specific sensor measures is in its datasheet.

BIn the networkIllustrative waveforms

  • Event · counted

    Voltage dip

    A short reduction in voltage, usually caused by a fault or a large load starting somewhere on the network.

  • Event · counted

    Voltage swell

    A short increase in voltage above the normal range.

  • Event · counted

    Interruption

    A loss of voltage, short or long.

  • Assessed over a period

    Harmonics

    Distortion of the voltage waveform at multiples of the supply frequency, mainly from non-linear loads.

  • Assessed over a period

    Flicker

    Repeated small voltage changes that cause visible variation in lighting.

  • Assessed over a period

    Unbalance

    Unequal voltages across the three phases.

  • Assessed over a period

    Frequency deviation

    Departure of the supply frequency from its nominal value.

  • Recorder

    Each event is recorded with its waveform.

    Before, during and after: the fault recorder function of a fixed analyser.

03Reading it

Rank the units. Describe the event.

AOil condition

Follow the trend, per unit
Oil in a healthy transformer changes slowly. A unit whose readings move faster than the rest of the population is the one to visit.
Moisture with temperature
Water moves between paper and oil as the transformer warms and cools. Compare like with like.
Rank, not diagnose
The sensor tells you which units need attention. An oil sample or an inspection tells you why.

BPower quality

Depth and duration
A dip is described by how far the voltage fell and for how long. Whether equipment rides through depends on both.
Direction
Recorded voltage and current together help show whether a disturbance came from the network or from the installation’s own load.
Statistics and events
Harmonics, flicker and unbalance are assessed statistically over a period. Dips, swells and interruptions are counted as events. A report needs both.
Comparability
Two instruments only agree if they measure the same way. That is what Class A is for.

04Can and cannot

What it can and cannot tell you.

An oil sensor is not a laboratory. An analyser sees only the point where it is installed.

What distribution transformer and power quality monitoring can and cannot tell you
It can tell youIt cannot tell you
Oil sensorThat oil condition in one unit is changing, and how fastOil sensorThe type of fault inside the transformer. It is not a DGA laboratory and not a partial discharge measurement
Oil sensorWhich units in a population to look at firstOil sensorThe condition of windings or tap changer directly
PQ analyserWhat the voltage did at this point, with time stamp and waveformPQ analyserWhat happened at points where nothing is installed
PQ analyserWhether supply at this point stayed within EN 50160 characteristicsPQ analyserWho is responsible for a disturbance, from one measuring point alone

Terms used on this page

Dielectric strength
The voltage the oil can withstand before it breaks down.
Point of common coupling
The point where a customer’s installation connects to the public network.
Class A
The measurement class in IEC 61000-4-30 for results that must be comparable between instruments.
Fault recorder
A function that captures waveforms before, during and after an event.
Non-linear load
A load that draws current which is not proportional to the voltage waveform.

A portable analyser answers a question after a problem has been noticed. A fixed analyser has already recorded the event when the question is asked.

07After an alarm

One sequence ends at the unit. The other ends at the table.

AOil condition

  1. 01 · Indication

    One unit moves off its baseline.

    One unit’s oil condition moves away from its own baseline.

  2. 02 · Compare

    Against load, temperature and similar units.

  3. 03 · Sample or inspect

    At the next opportunity.

    Take an oil sample or inspect the unit.

  4. 04 · Decide

    Treat, repair, replace or watch.

    Treat the oil, repair, replace or continue to watch.

BPower quality

  1. 01 · Event

    A dip, swell or interruption is recorded.

    With its waveform.

  2. 02 · Correlate

    Match the time stamp.

    With trips, process stops or equipment faults on site.

  3. 03 · Locate the source

    Network side or load side.

  4. 04 · Act

    With a record both sides can read.

    Raise it with the network operator, or address the load.

General sequences. Procedures and limits belong to the operator.

08Standards

Relevant standards

EN 50160
The voltage characteristics of public electricity networks.
IEC 61000-4-30
How power quality parameters are measured. Class A is the class used when results must be comparable and contractually reliable.
IEC 62586
Product standard for power quality measuring instruments; the source of the PQI-A-FI-H classification.

Standards are named for orientation.

10FAQ

Questions we are asked

Q1Why not fit a full monitoring system to every distribution transformer?

Because there are too many units and each is of modest value. The practical approach is one compact sensor per unit, used to rank the population.

Q2Is an in-oil sensor the same as DGA?

No. It is online oil-condition sensing. It indicates that the oil in a unit is changing. Laboratory analysis is still what explains why.

Q3What does Class A mean in practice?

That the instrument measures each parameter by the method defined in IEC 61000-4-30, so results from different Class A instruments can be compared and used in a contractual discussion.

Q4What is the difference between a power quality analyser and a fault recorder?

The analyser evaluates quality parameters over time. The fault recorder captures the waveform around an event. PQI-DA smart is described by its manufacturer as both.

Q5Where should a power quality analyser be installed?

Typically at the point of common coupling, on main busbars and on supplies to sensitive loads. The measuring points are defined for each installation.
